utterances.text: I'm not asking for an explanation at this moment. I just want to know for sure that you well understood that question whether you were considering that 16 is a number and that you have no reasons to believe that it was more. No question was asked about less. Whether you were aware of the question that was put to you, and you've answered that you had no reason to believe that there were more.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I stated here in my statement, I -- I hear from the other staff who were down there frequently saying that there is over 100 dead, and they don't have anywhere to store them any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Mr. Misetic, of course I'm not saying that your question was not correctly phrased in legal terms. At the same time, it appeared to me that the witness, although there was a correct formulation, might not have understood the gist of what was really asked of her and I would --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- like witnesses to know exactly what they're saying when they're asking your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I could just clarify. I may have been inarticulate enough that you also didn't understand what my point was, which was just to ask the witness having been a resident of Knin whether there may have been people whom she knew of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you also asked of unknown persons. If you would not have done that -- you were not limited your question to known persons I think. Let me just check but I think I re-read it. That's exactly -- let me just check --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The question I have at line -- line -- page 45, line 20, Your Honour, I believe I ended the question by saying, "...assuming of course that you know the names of such people."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. 45, line 15: "Are there any people that you know of by name or otherwise." Now, to me a fact that there is a body --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- is knowing otherwise. So therefore at least your questions then in this respect, if -- assuming of course if you know the names of such people is a bit in contradiction with your earlier question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: As I said before Your Honour I was a bit inarticulate and I apologise to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Just a note of clarification, Your Honour, on D69 I just slipped quickly through the B/C/S version and although my B/C/S is rather limited it seemed at least that at page 132 of D69 there are two more bodies that would have been found at the hospital, Bolnica Knin, I believe means Knin hospital; so I just clarify that maybe there are more than 16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps something for re-examination. Let's first wait and see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I can clarify, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: They are in sequential time order as to when they appeared, so I'm talking about the 4th and 5th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So let's move on and hear from the witness rather than from ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You said in your 1998 statement, Ms. Grubor, that the -- excuse me, that the RSK was bringing in wounded troops to the hospital; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: Wounded soldiers. Which -- which paragraph you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'll find it for you. I believe it's page 3 of your statement. Third paragraph. Towards the middle. You say: "It is difficult to say from where the wounded and the killed were brought in. I only know that they were brought in by RSK troops and UNPROFOR troops from the Kenyan Battalion."

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: Yeah, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, the RSK troops were bringing people in; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: They were bringing in soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know what kind of vehicles they were using to transport wounded?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: I would not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Were they military vehicles?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: I don't know. As I said, occasionally I would have a glance through the front door, but I was altogether probably once out of the hospital during all that event.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What you -- would that also be -- you say you occasionally would glance through the front door and you probably went out once during all that event. So you didn't have an opportunity then to actually see whether there was a tank outside the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: No. On that day, no, I haven't been outside. I was probably once, but it was just for a minute to help the person in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to show you another video. This is a video footage taken of the Knin hospital on the 5th, 6th and 7th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, this is 1D14-0146 and if it could be given a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any text?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit D70 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Grubor, do you recognise the building here? Not here, I mean in the video we watched.

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And what is that?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: I recognised the hospital in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And is that the way the hospital looked on the 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: I did not have a chance to look from that angle. During the day as I said, I did not go out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could reply the video. I'd like to stop at it one point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Grubor, is that the front entrance to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And off to the left there --

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Could you identify what that object is at the end of the walkway into the hospital there?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: That was a shield, I think, protecting from the wind or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What was the shield made out of?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Was it a form of glass?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: Not as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This car that you said pulled up with wounded on the 4th, can you tell the Court where that car was located when you said you looked through the door?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: If I looked through the door it is just lightly left from this shield but on the opposite side near the curb where the car-park was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So it would be on the outside part of the shield?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: Outside part of the shield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And so what angle then would -- let me ask a different question. Are you able -- when you're standing in the hospital, are you able to look through the shield and see what's -- what is on the outside of the shield?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: Not through the shield, but I can see on either side of the shield from inside the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And in your testimony earlier today, when a car pulled up had it already suffered damage or was it damaged at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: I did not see a car pulling up. After I hear what happened I went closer to the door and I could see there was a red car. In my recollection it was, you know, a hole or something like that, and I could see the hole in the back door, back passenger door. So I would not -- I did not witness that occurring, did you just out of curiosity I did look through the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you discuss in your statement the transfer of patients -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm again reminded if we could admit D68.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, D70. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, D70. You also more or less promised us to give us the background of this video material. This had seems to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Hrvatska television.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's called APTV, Your Honour, and we're in the process of disclosing it to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And APTV stands for Associated Press TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I have to admit I don't know Your Honour. I will check on the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes the Chamber would like to receive information about who produced that material or who broadcasted this. Please proceed. Yes, no objections against this video footage, Mr. Hedaraly?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No objection against D70, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection, so it is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry just a few more questions. As we're watching it, was there any damage to the Knin hospital that you know of from events that occurred on the 4th and the 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: At some stage on the afternoon, 4th of August, I did pick a shrapnel from the hospital stairwell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Where would that be located?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: It's -- there's -- there are the stairs that lead up to the upper floors, and I can't recall exactly which was it in between basement and ground floor that there were -- there was a broken glass and few shrapnels on the stairs. I picked one. I mean, I have even now that one back at my parents' place in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If you can tell us on any of these pictures of the outside of the hospital, would the staircase that you're talking about be on any of -- inside of any one of these windows, let's say?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: Not on this side. This is north side. The stairwell is on the south side of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If you see the location, please tell us to stop the video.

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: Just a moment. So completely on the opposite side from here. So that would be -- not this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We'll start it one more time and see if you see anything.

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: I did not see any of the -- I did not see to be recorded from southern side. That's -- that's still north side. This is also northern side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So it's on the south side of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: On south side of hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. In your 2007 statement, Ms. Grubor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, could we further explore this in some detail. You said you found shrapnel south side. Do you remember about -- you told us about shelling, et cetera. What we have seen now on these pictures relating to the 5th, the 6th, and apparently the 7th of August is the outside of the hospital which was exposed to shelling or fire. If at least you know which side was exposed to it, has that been shown on this video or has it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, which can you clarify the question. What was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which was exposed to the shelling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm trying to find out whether we saw a minute ago which where the images say it was the 5th and the 6th and the 7th of August whether that's true or not is still another matter, but whether the outside images of the hospital included those parts of the hospital so that to the extent your knowledge goes was exposed to fire of whatever kind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my opinion at the time, the shelling was coming from the mountain of Dinara, and which is positioned somewhere, let's say, east of the hospital and from the southern side which was from direction of the town Drnis. But that's just my opinion. I would not be 100 per cent sure about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And were those sides where as far as you could tell us the shelling did come from, were those side of the hospital shown on these images? That is if the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- fire would come from the south, it would be the south.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We saw here the west side of hospital and north side of hospital and not southern and east side of hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: 2007 statement, paragraph 2, you say: "I was told by Drazenka Koluvija, that 120 of the wounded," and now you're speaking about the night between the 4th act 5th, "maybe half many them were men in uniforms but I cannot be sure exactly, were taken out of the hospital during the night to Kravlja Draga a place where they intended to create a field hospital." Could you fell us why they were moving patients out of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: That's one of the things I was hearing from other staff. I did not play any part in making decisions or anything like that so all information that I have about that is from the other staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did the other staff tell you why patients were being moved out of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: During the day on 4th of August, majority of us were urging for some action to take away wounded as there was no any -- there was no any more place to put them in the basement. It was fully packed, and at the time we did not know how long it may last and how many more people we can expect, and lots of us there were urging for some action to be done for wounded to be taken away and to release pressure on hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, then on the morning of the 5th, 120 had been removed from the hospital; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Only 35 patients were left?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Why then did you have to move the patients out of the hospital into the UN camp? Let me ask a different question before I ask that. You said these 35 I believe in your statement you say in your statement at paragraph 2 there were 35 patients left behind in the hospital because they were not in a state where they could have gotten on the bus or the trucks. It's safe to say these were seriously wounded people?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: Yeah, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If now the hospital had only 35 people left and these people were so seriously wounded that they couldn't be transported by bus or by truck, why move them from the hospital to the UN compound?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: On the 5th of August, that was the second day, after so much shelling and bombing was going on we realised that we were not getting any more wounded. No one was coming to hospital. They did not have any security, any protection there at the hospital grounds. That was the time when we started talking about our personal security and security of our wounded to go somewhere to safe place. In fact, I myself was talking about leaving the place and following the other civilians which I saw leaving the town towards Bosnia and Serbia. In my belief something was wrong there, and we wanted to put wounded under UN protection rather than leaving them in hospital in case if Croatian soldiers come in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You did not want them to be taken as prisoners of war --

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: No, I wanted them to be under UN protection, not whatever happened them after.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, you were at the compound when Dr. Torbica was asking the UN to help him evacuate the patients. The UN in that discussion say that they don't have a mandate to move people from a hospital simply because you don't want them to fall in the hands of Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't understand what your question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In the conversation between Dr. Torbica and the UN?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did the personnel tell Dr. Torbica that the UN does not have a mandate to move seriously wounded patients from a hospital into their compound simply to help them avoid become prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: Probably Dr. Torbica would be relevant person to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You were present though and I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: As I said I did not understand English at the time, and as I said from hospital we wanted wounded to be taken to UN camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you participate in the convoys that then took patients from the hospital and into the UN camp?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: In which way participate?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Travel with the patients as they were being moved from the hospital and into the UN camp.

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many trips were made to evacuate the patients from the hospital and into the UN camp?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: Two trips.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Two trips. Do you know if any hospital staff went on these trips, these two trips?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: I -- in my recollection I don't think that anyone -- could be one person, but I'm not sure. Honestly, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Who -- as the first group of patients was being delivered to the UN compound was there any medical staff left with that group to provide medical attention to them that you know of?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: You mean in the UN camp?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In the UN camp, yes.

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't be able to answer that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know if the UN camp had any critical care facilities within it to be able to treat these patients?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: At the time I did not know. I guessed that they did, but I did not confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You spent some time in the camp afterwards. Did you subsequently find out what the capabilities were in the UN compound to provide care to wounded patients?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: I know they did have few staff down there, some type of -- I think Czech people were in charge of medical care, but I'm not sure what extent they were able to help.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. The next portion of your statement I wish to discuss is the death of Nikola Grujic. This is page 3 of your 1998 statement, the last paragraph. You say in the middle of the paragraph: "On Saturday morning a man named Grujic, first name unknown, arrived on foot to the hospital. He had been hit by shrapnel outside his house in Knin. He later died in hospital." Was Nikola -- sorry. Was this Grujic from Knin or did he live in Drnis?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: I have no idea. I just remember him walking in the hospital saying that he was -- that he received hit by shrapnel, and I have no idea where his house was or where he lived. I have nothing. I didn't even get his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you that he had been struck by shrapnel while standing outside the Tvik factory?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: I have no idea. He was urgently submitted down to the basement, and I don't know what his statement was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, he'd like to take you back to your transcript from today, page 24. Let me ask -- let me ask you some preliminary questions first. In your statement you say, again page 4, 1998, third paragraph -- sorry. Hold on. Page 3, second paragraph from the bottom. You say: "It was late Friday evening when I walked to the ECMM headquarters, which was nearby the hospital, to say good-bye to my friends, civilians from the neighbourhood." First, can you tell us why you felt the need to say good-bye?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: Before I come to that point, at about probably Friday at about 11.00 I ask friend of mine who worked in hospitals and was my flatmate at the time, I ask her to go home and have few hours of sleep.

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: A.m. -- p.m., sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: And so we had some discussion, and perhaps I stayed about couple or three hours more in the hospital trying to get her to come with me to have few hours of sleep, and when I walk back to the house I could not find any one of the people who live there, and I can't remember who exactly came over and said that all of them were in bomb shelter of ECMM building, which was only probably 200 metres away. So I went over to see them, and they and all of them were actually packed ready to leave the area. So I did say good-bye to them. They asked me to go, to leave the area with them, but I told them that I was obliged to go back to hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What time of day was -- was your visit to the ECMM headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: I -- I have no idea. It's hard to tell. All night was going chaotic, and I just know that I came back to hospital at about 5.00 in the morning. The visit to ECMM could be probably 2.00 in the morning or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And then you went home?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: I went home. I had probably one hour, couple of hours sleep at most and then went back to hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we could take a look at the map that the Prosecution used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: P57 is it, Mr. Registrar? 58, P58.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Grubor, you've identified certain locations on this map which you say you saw were shelled, and then in your testimony this morning you said that most of these locations you saw from your vantage point at the hospital; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: Yeah, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you identify for us which of these numbers you saw from a vantage point other than the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: Number 8 is -- you mean just to identify what is the location?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No. I'm saying did -- is every location here what you saw from your vantage point at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: I would say I could see -- for example, I did not circle the road leaving out of the town, which was also bombed, which is known as Buljina Strana.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Maybe I'm not being clear enough. Is it fair to say that all of the locations that you've circled here are things you saw from your perspective at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: I can't say that I could see every single one well. However, it is more in my view or recollection the places that were slightly rised were hilly areas were more observed. I could see explosions in the town, but because of town is low, I could not tell exact location of that, while these elevated areas like number 10 or 8 or this road leaving the town is much easier to see effect of explosions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask -- ask it this way: This morning you said you saw a shoe store had been hit because you were driving by that shoe store; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Are any of the locations on this map things that you saw as you were standing next to or passing by that location?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: You mean location. Is that the shoe store that I saw --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No. Let's talk specifically. On the map, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11.

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: Yeah, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Are 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, and 11 all things that you saw from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: I saw the explosions on these areas, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, and 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But you saw them from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: I could see most of them from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You say most of them. Are any of them things that you saw from a location other than the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: Just a moment. Number 6 is the location that I was driving by. I did not see bomb fell onto that building, but I saw that building being destroyed, which my common sense told me that it was due to a bomb felling on that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That is what you referred to as the shoe store this morning?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: Yes. Or, for example, number 4, which is the police station. I did not see. That was during the night-time. It was just direction where it was coming from where I could see big fire, big blaze, but I did not see exact building which was --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: -- hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm just -- for the purposes of these questions, number 6 was what you saw as you were driving past it; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: Yeah, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How about 7, 8, 9, 10, and 11?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: Number 7 I could see that clearly from hospital. It was quite close. Number 8 -- just a moment. Number 8, I also had a good view of this one because it is elevated just below castle. Number 9 -- just a moment. Where is number 9? Yeah. Number 9 is just -- it is below hospital, quite close, and I could see explosions there -- there frequently all day. Number 10, it's the place that is slightly elevated, but I can -- I did not have clear view of this one. It was just the location that I could see explosions. I can't tell that I saw actual houses, that I had that clear view of that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, you note on number 10 to the left you see what's to the let of number 10?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is it possible that what you saw was the Knin army barracks?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: I saw that part -- that part being bombed. I saw explosions within army barracks compounds, but also I did see a side of the -- of that in number 10, explosions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now. If we could show you another video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the number ready, Mr. ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We've had a discussion with Mr. Registrar. This relates to some material that was raised for the first time in direct and so there are no numbers yet, but we will deal with it as soon as we can. It's something we've now come up during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless I take it that we've already assigned a number to material which is not yet uploaded.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This becomes Exhibit D71 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Grubor, if you could watch this clip closely and see if you can see a building which you think may be the shoe store.

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: I believe it just passed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: I think this was the supermarket. I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We'll go back, and tell us when to stop the tape.

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: That's the building, but I believe that just before this passage on the left that there was a shoe store, in my recollection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, that's the one on the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The one with the pink orange paint or the one with the yellow?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: I think that's the one with the pink orange, but I'm not 100 per cent sure. I think that's the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at this one and what I would suggest you -- play it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is that the shoe store?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: I can't be 100 per cent sure. I still believe it was the other one, but could be this one as well. That's the building next to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What about that one on the end? Could that also be the shoe store?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: I think this -- this corner building was the restaurant here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's play this clip back, and if you could now tell us where you saw a building destroyed by shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Because you yourself were travelling by car.

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: I was travelling by car, and here on the left in my recollection, as far as I can remember, it was this orange building. I may be wrong, but I do remember seeing on the left. I am pretty sure it was just above the shoe store. But as I said, you know, there is very small chance that I could miss the building one for another. But as I said again, pretty sure that's the orange building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We will submit that this video was shot by reporters entering Knin on the 7th of August. And so what I'm trying to ascertain is if you say on this road you saw the shoe store had been damaged by artillery fire.

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: Not shoe store damaged by artillery fire. I said when I look up the window one of these upper floor windows, I could see the hole in the ceiling. I don't know was it due to bomb felling or tank firing. I just saw that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So you don't know --

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: -- damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You saw a broken window?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: And saw the ceiling, big hole in the ceiling. I could see the sky from the window up through the building. I believe it was the result of artillery fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, also in your statement you were asked some questions by the Presiding Judge about the fact that you weren't sure on the morning of the 4th whether the artillery fire was Serbs firing onto Croatian positions or Croatian positions firing into Knin; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Would it be fair then to say then that the shelling was not anywhere near your apartment, at that point at least?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: The loud noise, shelling, was the reason I woke up. It was 5.00 in the morning. And when I got up and looked through the window, I could see explosions. As my window is towards east, I could see explosions I would say probably 2, 300 metres away from the house, and then I realised that Knin was under fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. While we still have the map up, if I could just ask you, you said as you -- when you were going into the UN camp for the second time in your statement it says you swam across two rivers?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: Yeah, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you explain why you didn't use that -- what appears to be a railway track over that first river?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: At the time I was scared all the time. I was running. I saw about probably 20 tanks when I wanted to cross the road. I had to wait for them to pass going into the city from Vrlika direction. I took this road next to the railway station because that was -- no one was using that. It was out of the way, out of the sight for safety reasons. When I came to this bridge, which is long bridge down there, the first river is a little one. It's easy to cross that river regardless whether using a bridge or swimming across. When I approach the bridge I could see people up there at the castle of Knin. I was afraid that there maybe soldiers with snipers. I did not want to be visible. I decided to take this, let's say shortcut rather than going long way across the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. You discuss seeing a tractor -- you discuss the explosion of a tractor near the UN compound in your statement.

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: Yeah. That's labelled on this map number 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Right. Now, in your 2007 statement you said in paragraph 3 that you did not actually see what happened there; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: It's -- if I bring myself back there, all of that was too terrifying and horrifying. That was the moment when I did not believe it is happening, and my mind refuse to take in any more. It was just so much horror. When we approach this convoy and bomb fell down, I immediately told to Dr. Igor, "What do we do? Do we stop here and do we help these people?" And his replay was, "We can't do anything." I had seen already lots of blood. I was literally trying to shut my eyes and pass that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could go to 1D14-0194.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I seek some clarification? The question was put to you that you did not actually see what happened there. You gave an answer which you described your state of mind. Is that now to say that you saw the spot after what had happened or that you did see it? It's not entirely clear to me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw the actual bomb to fell onto the convoy. I did see people felling off the tractor. However, as immediately that was probably 50 metres away, or 100 metres at most. I discussed with doctor whether we should stop and try to help the people, to which he said, "There is no way we can do anything. We are now just to take care of the people from hospital." So that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just stop you there. So I have understood you well that you have corrected now your 2007 statement in which you say that you did not actually see it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which paragraph is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "I didn't see the shell hit, but there were shells falling all around."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was -- this must be the one that was referring outside the UN camp. This one shell, explosion, was just ahead of us as we were facing that direction, driving along the road towards UN camp. So that would be probably about 100 metres at most from UN camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but now did you see the shell hit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So to that extent you're correcting what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, did see the shell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just wanted to make clear what your position is. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In terms of what you say you saw, you then say in your statement you saw a huge explosion from one the trailers; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: Which part are you referring?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 3, the last sentence. This is of your supplemental --

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: Just a moment. Yeah. Not from -- sorry. I just did not read this. I saw a huge explosion just outside the UN camp. I saw also bomb felling on the convoy. There were two bombs, separate bombs, on -- just down there. One was when one bomb fell onto the convoy of people were there. The other one, huge explosion, was just outside of the UN gates, which is just on the other side of the road, which was outside UN camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And the people that were killed were in military uniform?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: That's -- I wouldn't be able to answer that. In my opinion that was convoy of civilians who were coming from direction of Drnis, from those villages in my -- I presume who were waiting for the shelling to stop and to pass the town to exit the other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Could we go to page 2, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is this the perspective from the camp to that crossroads where this incident took place?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: This is still this road, and at the end of this road there is main road which is coming from the left down towards the town. So this is side road which we are looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct. But you would have been on this road looking in that direction from this perspective?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: That events that I am talking about, I was on my way to here. I would be looking this direction towards us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 1 now, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, could you -- yes. Could you also -- you're showing photographs and you're asking the witness all kinds of things about it but the Chamber of course there's also some objective information in that photograph, that is which direction it was taken, of course the Chamber in order to follow the testimony -- oh, that comes now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's what I'm showing you now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You see the UNCRO barracks is marked on the screen. The picture was taken from the red dot there, and the incident took place in the area that's circled number 14?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: It was farther down. It was before this crossing. It was towards the city. It was coming from the opposite direction from the town, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry, let me clarify something. When you say farther down do you mean on the roads towards the red dot in this picture?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we ask the witness to use the cursor so that we -- what is further down that we know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say it was towards down here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This -- somewhere down here. So it was about 100 metres from the UN camp, which is the very crossing here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we first ask how you approached the UN camp, or what was -- how were you moving, from where to where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was coming from hospital through the town towards UN camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then on this photograph where -- by which road did you enter the area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This road. This area here I was travelling towards UN camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could you then please move the cursor in the direction which you are -- that was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the way that I was going that morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Just for the record the witness with the cursor shows that she moved on a small road starting at the top left-hand corner going in -- in 4.00 direction down towards. Yes, that's clear. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to page 3, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise these pictures as the individuals who were killed in this incident?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Were you able to see the individuals?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: I was, but I did not look.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I believe there's one more page, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, in this picture it looks -- the person on the bottom picture looks to be wearing some sort a camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: During the wartime all males from -- they're required to be in military service so I am not surprised at all. And plus --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Grubor, you're more or less now explaining. The question was simply whether that was usual thing to where is another matter which the Chamber might have to consider, but as a witness of fact you're now invited to answer this question whether what you see is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- someone wearing a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's the uniform that RSK soldiers were wearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall on that date when you saw these individuals were they wearing camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, if you saw this incident, did the big explosion that you referred to in your statement, were there weapons on the trailer that -- that exploded, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: That's too much to ask. I have of no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could ask for a number for this exhibit and tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'd like to have the series of photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course the Chamber is interested to know where this material comes, what it depicts, taken by whom, when, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: These are pictures produced to us by the Prosecution and taken by Mr. Alun Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- and when or --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: He had labels on them. We took the labels off but he labelled them as incident close to the UN compound on the 5th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Not necessarily the one the witness described or --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, Your Honour, there's only one incident, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I thought I heard you say incidents, but looking at the transcript I see them as incident, an incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, just one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: To the extent it is marked, Your Honour, that's fine but if we are going to discuss the admissibility of it the Prosecution would have some objections to this document. The first one is on the first page where it says area where I witnessed a shell killed. I mean if that's Mr. Roberts, I think it may be -- would be better to be shown to Mr. Roberts. These pictures were shown to Ms. Grubor. She talks about an incident, pictures were shown to her, she says she's not sure those are the same pictures; so for that reason I think maybe we can mark it for identification but maybe to tender it is perhaps to wait when we confirm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I -- as a matter of fact, I invited the registrar to arrange for a meeting together with legal officer to see how to deal with marked for identification, because this witness -- some of the photographs are certainly relevant if only because the witness says how she travelled at that time, whereas others might be of that incident, might not be of that incident. At least the witness could not confirm that. This series then for the time being remain marked for identification pending further decisions on the matter. Yes, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: One clarification, Your Honour, that language that we put in there we took straight out of the Prosecution's map which they've used as P58 and that's the location at least that we thought is marked as 14 and in her words placed where I saw a shell killed several civilians 5 August 1995. So we just put it on a Google map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we go back to that -- to that first one with the text on it? Mr. Registrar, is there anyway to -- yes. It says area. That is fully congruent with what the witness said, isn't it. So therefore will that objection stand or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I may just clarify with the witness that this is exactly the same location as on P58 that she's mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think as a matter of fact she testified how she arrived there, so therefore it should not be too much doubt about that. Matters remain marked for identification and we'll see what to do with it. Then, Mr. Misetic, you said that this picture would answer my question as to from where the photograph was taken. Of course it only says where the photo was taken, not in what direction, but I take it then it's on the picture it's to the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit D72 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and keeps that status for the time being. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to finish by the second break time going to try to move quickly through this. If I could show you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, a video this is 1D14-0181.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And you in your statement discuss the behaviour of Croatian troops as they arrived in -- in the hospital on the 5th, and I'd like to show you two videos of Dr. Torbica. One is on the 5th of August as he's met which Croatian forces, and the second is a statement he made concerning the same events one month later in the -- while he was being filmed by the UN in the UN compound so let's see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, are the two footages one exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No they're separate exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First one then Mr. Registrar would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D73 marked for identification, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I could first ask you Ms. Grubor is that, in fact, Dr. Torbica?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] We have no information. Is there anyone left at the hospital? We don't know, there's no one left here at the hospital. There is no one at the hospital we're looking for them but we don't know where they are. Doctor, tell us about the condition of your patients. At this moment we don't know anything about the situation but as far as the wounded persons are concerned the Croatian army's behaviour's truly correct, and we hope that it will remain that way. They act properly I would like to commend these boys from Varazdin they behaved very correctly."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One moment, please. We are considerably behind with the French translation. Therefore, I think the last portion that was translated was whether that in fact that was Dr. Torbica where the witness confirmed that it was. Have you provided the text of this video, the transcript to the booth? Then I'd like to have it in its entirety replayed and then wait until the end until the French translation has caught up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Dr. Torbica: I'm the only one who stayed. Fuck it, everyone else escaped. I stayed here with the wounded with these poor people here. Dr. Zdilar: Are you a surgeon? Dr. Torbica: Yes, I am. Dr. Zdilar: You have a degree? Dr. Torbica: Sure I do. What happened to Josko? We have no information about their whereabouts. Dr. Zdilar: Is there any one left at the hospital? Dr. Torbica: We do don't know. There's no one left at the hospital. Dr. Zdilar: There's no one at the hospital? Dr. Torbica: No we are looking for them, but we don't know where they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, tell us about condition of your patients? Dr. Torbica: At this moment we don't know anything about the situation but as far as the wounded persons are concerned, the Croatian army's behaviour is truly correct, and we hope that it will remain that way. They act properly. I would like to commend these boys from Varazdin. They behaved very correctly. Dr. Zdilar: You want a smoke? Dr. Torbica: But I did not remember their names. I'm sorry I didn't remember their names so I could ... their really nice guys.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: You're a surgeon? Dr. Torbica: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Do you only have surgical patients or other patients as well? Dr. Torbica: Only surgical ones. I'm a surgeon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: You're the only member of the hospital staff who stayed with the patients? Dr. Torbica: You should turn to this side. Listen ... Dr. Zdilar (to the cameraman): As a doctor only speak for myself I do my job on my own behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Dr. Torbica: Thank you."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That was Dr. Torbica in front of the UN compound; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: Yeah, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd also like to show you a video of Dr. Torbica approximately one month later being interviewed by the United Nations in the UN camp, again talking about the treatment by the Croatian forces upon entry into the hospital. Again, Your Honour, I need -- sorry, let me call it up. It is 1D14-0180. If we could get a number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar that would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit D74 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: "Dr. Torbica: Heavy shelling UN performed two evacuations. We were waiting for the third evacuation APC -- APC convoy to start, but at that point Croats had already penetrated the town. We were understandably very afraid at that point but first group of Croatian soldiers who entered the hospital were very polite. I awaited them and told them to sit down. We had no problems with them. I want to reiterate that they were behaving in quite an orderly way. And the -- and the soldiers made it possible for me to enter the UN camp with all -- and join the patients which were evacuated earlier."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Grubor, did the Croatian forces behave correctly when they entered the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: I did not meet them then. They entered the hospital, I hear the shooting upstairs, and I hear explosion which I presumed was a bomb, but that's all I know. I left before they came downstairs to the bomb shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You're just then recounting simply what you heard, but you didn't actually see any Croatian soldiers mistreating anyone in the hospital; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: No, I didn't see. And I have to admit later from -- I heard from Dr. Torbica that no one was killed in that accident -- in that incident when they entered the hospital, but however I did hear shooting, and I did hear explosion from just upstairs basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could ask to have the video exhibits admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objection to 73 and 74?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: There are no objection, Your Honour. I would just like to note that is date superimposed on D73, and there's just -- the video itself doesn't refer to that date but subject to that clarification we have no objection on D73 and D74.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And D73 and D74 are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Grubor did you file an incident report with anyone in the UN compound that Croatian forces were shooting at people in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: As soon as I arrived to the UN camp, I did tell what happened. I can't tell that I was in a very good state. However, I asked them to about and to protect people in hospital. I told them that Croatian soldiers entered the hospital, and I urged them to go and send someone to protect people who were left there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this might be -- in light of one answer she has given, I have maybe one document that I'd like to retrieve during the break and ask for a question about that one document and then I will be finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will have a break then, but could I also get some information from the Cermak and Markac Defence on how much time they would need tore cross-examination? Mr. Kay for Mr. Cermak or Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Nothing arises at the moment that requires further questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, General Markac's Defence will need one hour at the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we will have a break and we'll resume at 10 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could call up 65 ter 0121.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit D75 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You can see from the cover page this is an UNCIVPOL report. I'm afraid the date is not clear on the cover page, Your Honour. There's a faxed line on the bottom of that page that says it was faxed at 8/8, but I'm sure of the date of the actual drafting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: The B/C/S version does have a date at the top which on English version we can't read properly. It says 8th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Then the question is on what that is based, but let's -- let's -- I see that at least the document appears to have been faxed already on the 8th of August. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could turn to the next page, please. Beginning at point 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If you could read that, Ms. Grubor, until the portion that is blacked out, and let me know when you've finished reading. Have you finished reading?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You'll note at the third paragraph it says: "As the soldiers stormed into the said ward, one of the nurses escaped through the exit door leaving the rest side ..." Do you know if that refers to you?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: " ... and on seeing the soldiers, they started screaming and asking for drinking water. The soldiers ordered one the persons to give them water and was overheard saying that that was the last drip of water for them and further that the soldiers were to administer the last injection (meaning massacre)." Now, before the break you said you spoke to people in the UN camp. Do you know if you were the source of that information in this UNCIVPOL report?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: No, I could not. I left before Croatian soldiers entered, came into the shelter, so definitely not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would ask that it be tendered as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This was marked for identification as D75.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and D75 is admitted under evidence in the absence of any objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Kay, your position remains as it was before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No questions. Okay, Mr. Mikulicic. You will be questioned by Mr. Mikulicic who is Defence for Mr. Markac. Please begin, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mrs. Grubor.

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I would ask you a few questions and I would appreciate if you would answer to the best of your recollection. Your first statement was given on the 3rd of April, 1998 in the liaison office of the United Nations in Belgrade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you were getting in contact with the UN office and giving your statement, were you assisted in any way by the Veritas office in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. They -- in fact, they were not aware that I was giving a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that answer. In your statement you said you had been employed with the Knin hospital as a laboratory assistant. Can you tell us precisely what kind of duties did you have?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: I was working in microbiology laboratory for the period of last ten years prior to the event on 4th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what kind of training did you have for that position?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: All of us are familiar with the system, schooling system, in former Yugoslavia. I got my degree in -- for laboratory assistant in microbiology in medical school in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In addition to that training did you have any additional skills, some other schooling you had completed?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Grubor, there has been discussion about this, but I want to ask you a direct question. Do you know that the Supreme Defence Council and Milan Martic in the republics of Krajina proclaimed a state of war in the month of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, this has been asked to the witness. The within has answered it. If -- unless there's any specific reason why you would like to go over that same ground again please do so if there is any specific reason. If there's not, however, there's no reason to deal with the matter again. Similar observation in relation to the education of a laboratory assistant. If there's a good reason to expect that this laboratory assistant would not have proper training, then of course you can ask about her -- ask about it. If, however, this is a laboratory assistant which received the usual training for a laboratory assistant, then of course there's no need to go over that unless again if there's any specific reason which might raise our eyebrows, then you certainly should do it. But if it's just to seek verification that this woman was trained -- this witness was trained for the job she did, then of course there's no need to ask that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. To continue my examination, I will explain why I have asked these questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Grubor, you mentioned in your statement that the attack in the morning of the 4th was sudden and unexpected, because if it had been expected you at the hospital would have proceeded to implement an existing plan. Can you tell us exactly what kind of plan existed at the hospital for such contingencies?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: In my recollection, at the beginning of civil war in former Yugoslavia, so that would be in 1990, all of us had a meeting, let's say, and were tasked to take a part in case of unexpected, meaning that some -- that emergency -- in case of emergency the hospital would be ran downstairs in the bomb shelter. So I would say that some of us were supposed to take some medications or some necessary equipment down in order to be able to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me go back to your statement from 1998 in which you stated that some of the employees of the hospital remained - that's page 2, last paragraph - remained to work at the hospital while others left. Do you know how it came about that some of the medical personnel stayed with the patients while others left? What were the reasons? Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: I don't understand which medical personnel you referred to, who stayed with the wounded and who were the ones who left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let me point out page 2 of your statement, the paragraph before last which contains a list of staff members who were in hospital on Friday and who remained to work there after the offensive. Can you confirm that these were the people who stayed at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: Yeah, those are the people. If you are referring to the others who left the hospital during the night, I'm -- on Friday to Saturday, they left with the wounded who were evacuated from hospital during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Grubor, I would now like you to watch a video clip dated 6 August, the day when the hospital was handed over. 000180.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] The hand-over. "Dr. Zdilak: Today at 12.30, the Croatian army is handing over the general hospital in Knin to the civilian health care authorities. Twenty health care workers have been sent from Zadar, and they are going to start working now. "Dr. Viskovic: We found here some seven to eight health care workers of Serb ethnicity who stayed with the patients at their own free will and they joined our team. They will be working together with us. They will fare exactly as we do. We are all professionals. We are blind to differences in ethnicity or religion. All patients are equal in our eyes, and we must treat them all as professionals."

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Grubor -- could we get a number from the registry first?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour this becomes Exhibit D76 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objection against D76? No objection. D76 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On this recording we saw the newly appointed administrator of the hospital, Dr. Ante Viskovic. Did you know that man from before?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it the case that the administrator of the Knin hospital before Dr. Viskovic was Dr. Igor Torbica?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: I am just trying to remember. It has been 13 years since then, but at the time it was another surgeon. His name was Dusan -- I can't remember last name. I may remember later on, but can't -- can't think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Never mind. Thank you, Mrs. Grubor. If you don't remember, we will not insist on that. Could we now play another video clip, 3D0002120, recorded on the next day, on the 7th of August.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Life and work have started to normalise at the Knin hospital today. Health care minister of Republic of Croatia, Andrija Hebrang visited the hospital grounds as they are being cleaned up. "Dr. Hebrang: Well, the civilian authorities have entered this health care facilities as you can see and found the same problems we see everywhere in newly liberated areas, a mess, a mess, and more mess. The first thing they did when they came was to make Serb patients comfortable provide them with adequate care and thus demonstrated the civilized ways of the Croatian state when it comes into its own territory. "Reporter: At the hospital, we also found nine health care workers of Serb ethnicity who had chosen to stay here of their own free will to care for the 22 Serb patients. 40 patients had been taken away by the UNPROFOR and they are unaware of their current status."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Grubor -- I'm sorry, Your Honours. I have to pay more attention to interpretation. Mrs. Grubor, we have seen this person before, earlier today. Do you recognise him in this freeze?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you tell it us for the record who it is?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: Goran Jejina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We can continue.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Many are in a difficult condition because surgery could not be performed on time due to objective reasons. So we hope that in the future, in the near future, this will be resolved and the patients will receive the best possible care. "Reporter: Although order is being restored at the hospital extremely rapidly so that seriously-ill Serb patients have already been transferred from the inhumane conditions in the basement and towards upstairs, the offices of Serb doctors who had fled had not yet been entered into. It is said that sappers will be called in for that job."

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Grubor, after these events at the UN camp where you said you took cover, did you have occasion to speak to your colleagues who worked at the hospital after it was taken over by Croatian civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: A couple weeks after I spoke to Drazenka who came over to the UN camp as well as a few others who decided to stay. I met them probably six months to one year after in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did these people share with you any information that would indicate that Croatian authorities were improper in their treatment of Serb health care workers?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: The only thing that I hear that was that one of wounded soldiers died is he was too late to receive medical care, and I think that was referring to this soldier named Grujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand. Mrs. Grubor, you described for us today how seriously wounded people were evacuated in UN vehicles in two trips from the Knin hospital. I'm now referring to your statement from 2007, page 2, paragraph 4. You said that UN vehicles followed your ambulance because they feared they could be attacked by soldiers of the army of Serbian in Krajina. Can you clarify this?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: At the time of attack UN were -- sorry. The whole area was under UN protection for the last two or three years. Therefore, the people felt that UN failed them for such horrible things taking place under the UN protection. And therefore, UN ask us to lead the way and to advise any soldier that was left in that town, I mean RSK soldier, to let them know that we are going to transport wounded from hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one clarification. In this one line where it reads: "The UN vehicles were following our ambulances because they were worried about being shot," could you tell us who you refer to by the word "they"? Was it people from the UN vehicles or from the ambulances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People from the UN vehicles were worry -- worrying about being shot at the time. There was only us in ambulance vehicle, me and doctor, and behind us there were three UN transporters who were supposed to evacuate the wounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At the beginning you described the training you had and your duties at the hospital, and you said you had no other training. I will now show you a passage from your statement of 1998, page 4, paragraph 1, where you stated that in Knin there were no military positions of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and therefore you thought that the shelling of the town was absolutely illegitimate, without any legal justification. Mrs. Grubor, may we conclude that you were not qualified, actually, to give such an assessment, such an evaluation of the shelling of the town in view of your position and your occupation?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: I did not come here as an expert in any field, including my own field. My statement was based on all events that took place, on information that was exchange in between us, and what I saw within few days prior to this event. So that was my conclusion, or let's say common sense out of all of this, but I am not qualified to say that I am an expert to give expert opinion about any military moments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I asked this because I thought you may have heard someone else make this qualification, so let me ask you directly. Was there anyone around you with whom you were in contact who had shared with you this conclusion that you refer to in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MIRA GRUBOR
utterances.text: Within few days prior to this event I had a number of my male friends, people who told me that they were to be taken to Bosnia, and therefore I got an opinion that as I couldn't see any serious number of soldiers in the very town, that all of them were taken over to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will move on from this subject. Now, Mrs. Grubor, I want to show you the last video clip filmed on the 8th of August. It's 3D000201.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but perhaps we should first assign a number to the previous one, Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Registrar, the previous one would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that becomes Exhibit D77 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D77. Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: None. Just for the record I like to note that is date superimposed and the video itself does not provide any date on when it was filmed but subject to that there are no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- then D77 is admitted into evidence. This new one, Mr. Registrar, would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this becomes Exhibit D78 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let us look at the clip.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Mr. Roncevic: The birth of a first baby born in liberated Knin which is not only symbolic, it has a special weight and importance. Here is a story of this hospital from Josko Martinovic. "Mr. Martinovic: It is born. It is 51 centimetres long and has no name as yet but our technicians nicknamed her Mirna from Knin. Her mother, 25-year old Mirjana Vujko had been too afraid to leave the UNCRO barracks therefore Croatian obstetrician, Dr. Lozo, had come to perform the delivery afterwards however the new mother changed her mind and the Knin hospital admitted its youngest patient. "Journalist: Was everything all right with you? "Mother: Yes. "Journalist: Here is the little baby, a girl. "Journalist: The beginning of her life coincided with the activation of Knin's general hospital. This hospital now has a one-to one ratio of medical personnel and patients, 30 of each, but numbers are growing by the hour.
